extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and practitioners interested in scientific method and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for forming, testing, and accepting scientific hypotheses and for explaining observed laws by deduction from more general laws. Focuses on the proper use of hypotheses, the Deductive Method, and standards of verification (e.g., Method of Difference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive Method (induction + ratiocination + verification)
rubrics_metrics.description: To discover the cause of any phenomenon by the Deductive Method the process must consist of three parts: induction, ratiocination, and verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induction: ascertain the laws of the causes (or obtain premises); Ratiocination: compute from those laws the expected effect in the particular case; Verification: compare the calculated effect with the actual phenomenon. No one of these three parts can be dispensed with; their order is induction → ratiocination → verification (though discovery order may differ). Example: Newton's proof that the same attraction that governs the moon causes fall of bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of the Hypothetical Method
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hypothetical Method suppresses the first step (induction) and proceeds by ratiocination and verification from an assumed law; it is legitimate only when verification fulfills the conditions of a complete induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Hypothetical Method is acceptable if the verification is such that a false law could not lead to the true result — i.e., the verification must rule out all alternative laws capable of producing the same consequences. Newton's derivation of planetary forces is given as an example where the hypothetical assumption became proven because no other hypothesis could accord with the facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of unique deductive consequence for hypothesis verification
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis can be accepted by hypothetical deduction only if no other law except the assumed one can lead deductively to the same conclusions which the hypothesis leads to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification must supply both the affirmative and the negative instances required by the Method of Difference so that the assumed law is shown uniquely responsible for the phenomenon; otherwise the hypothetical assumption remains unproved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference (affirmative and negative instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification that fulfills induction conforms to the canon of the Method of Difference: one must obtain both the affirmative instance (A B C → a b c) and the negative instance (B C → b c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both instances may be obtained by experiment or by prior deduction; it is sufficient that they be obtained. Newton's case generated the required instances by deduction. Without the negative instance (showing that omission of the assumed antecedent removes the effect) the verification is incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis: proper definition and role
rubrics_metrics.description: An hypothesis is any supposition made (either without actual evidence, or on evidence avowedly insufficient) to deduce conclusions in accordance with known facts, used to enable the Deductive Method to be earlier applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses serve to explain by resolving a complex law into simpler ones; they are invented to allow deduction where induction is incomplete. But being suppositions, they must later be submitted to legitimate induction for acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of hypotheses (plausibility & analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses are philosophically proper when allied by analogy with known laws or when they supply plausibility; wholly arbitrary or fanciful hypotheses lack the plausibility of those related to known phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two common kinds: (1) a real phenomenon whose law is supposed (law unknown) and (2) a fictitious agent supposed to act according to known laws. Either kind is historically used (e.g., Newton's assumed inverse-square law, Descartes' vortices). But hypotheses should not be invented solely because they make explanation easy; they should be testable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of subsequent testing by legitimate induction
rubrics_metrics.description: For an hypothesis to be received as a truth of nature (and not a mere technical help), it must be capable of being tested by the canons of legitimate induction and must actually be submitted to that test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial status as hypothesis is provisional; verification by induction (experiments or derivable negative/affirmative instances) is required before an hypothesis attains the status of an accepted law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation: ultimate laws vs derivative laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between derivative laws (deducible from and resolvable into more general laws) and ultimate laws (which cannot be so resolved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific progress often consists in resolving derivative laws into more general laws, but there must exist ultimate laws; identification of derivative laws moves us closer to ultimate ones. One should assess whether a candidate law is derivative (and thus open to resolution) or ultimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower bound on ultimate laws (sensory distinctions principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate laws of nature cannot be fewer than the distinguishable sensations or feelings of our nature; each distinguishable quality (e.g., each color) requires at least one ultimate law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because certain phenomena (like color) are qualitatively distinct from others, explanations will eventually require laws specific to those qualities; this limits how far reduction can proceed. When evaluating claims of total reduction, check whether qualitatively distinct phenomena have been truly subsumed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for instances where a general law applies (deductive prediction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a law is experimentally established, deduce where its necessary conditions occur and search for fresh instances in which those conditions meet to test or illustrate the law (e.g., Faraday's deduction about conductors moving in earth's magnetic field).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the established general law to predict and look for cases (in various regions/types) where its conditions hold; such targeted searches can yield novel confirmations or explanations of phenomena (e.g., Aurora Borealis speculation, equatorial vs polar differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding illegitimate explanatory assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The weak point in some explanatory attempts is assuming the existence of an entity or mechanism without evidence solely because it facilitates explanation (e.g., assuming an unproven vibrating fluid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses invoking unobserved entities should be treated cautiously; their existence must be justified beyond explanatory convenience. Prefer hypotheses that either posit real agents or at least suppose agents acting according to known laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of resolution: when resolution is legitimate
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolving observed laws into more general laws is legitimate when it diminishes complexity by showing the observed law arises from simpler, known modes of production (as with motion, electricity, magnetism examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the candidate resolution actually reduces the number or complexity of independent laws, and whether it leaves a residual ultimate law that still must be acknowledged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification can be obtained by deduction or experiment (nature of evidence immaterial)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is immaterial whether the two instances required for the Method of Difference are obtained by experiment or by a prior deduction; what matters is that they be obtainable and provide assurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluation, consider both empirical and logically deduced instances as legitimate forms of verification, provided they meet the methodological standards (unique consequence, negative instance, etc.).
